title: Practical organ-on-a-chip platform helps assess the toxicity of environmental chemicals
byline: Seoul National University of Science and Technology
excerpt: Among the thousands of chemicals used in daily life, toxicity information is available for only a small fraction. Much of this information comes from high-dose animal studies, which are costly, time-consuming and limited by species differences.
content_html:
Among the thousands of chemicals used in daily life, toxicity information is available for only a small fraction. Much of this information comes from high-dose animal studies, which are costly, time-consuming and limited by species differences.

Organ-on-a-chip (OOC) systems use microfluidics to mimic human tissue and organ physiology, offering a more human-relevant approach to toxicity testing. However, their application to toxicological assessment remains challenging due to issues with usability, flow control and biological replication. Complex tubing in flow-based OOC systems can further complicate their implementation.

To address these challenges, a research team involving professor Ki-Tae Kim and doctoral candidate Jiyun Kang from the Department of Environmental Engineering at Seoul National University of Science and Technology (SeoulTech) has developed a modular liver-on-a-chip (LOC) platform designed specifically for environmental toxicological assessment.

"The use of organ-on-a-chip platforms for environmental chemical assessment has advanced slowly, since testing many chemicals at multiple concentrations puts different demands on the system," explains Kim. "Our study offers insights into how these issues can be resolved and where these systems could be useful."

Their study was published in Environmental Science & Technology on Sept. 15, 2026.

Tubing-free chips with controlled flow

The proposed LOC platform accommodates 12 cartridge-based chips in parallel. It features a tubing-free design, with each chip incorporating an easy-to-use clamping-based sealing mechanism. A single LOC chip contains human liver HepG2 cultures and features independent unidirectional recirculating flow, with the flow rate and shear stress determined by gear-based peristaltic pumping.

Unlike static plate-based cultures, this recirculating flow continuously exposes cells to the circulating medium and enables controlled, reproducible chemical exposure, better reflecting biological conditions.

Liver responses at lower chemical concentrations

In tests, the LOC platform demonstrated stronger hepatic function than static plate cultures, with markedly higher expression of CYP1A2, CYP3A4 and CYP2E1 mRNA. The researchers used the LOC platform to evaluate the hepatotoxicity of triphenyl phosphate (TPhP), a common flame retardant used in household items with known links to liver toxicity.

During experiments, the cartridge modules demonstrated high reproducibility and uniform chemical distribution. In response to TPhP exposure, the platform showed changes in levels of hepatic phenotypic markers, including urea, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Notably, these altered responses were observed at lower measured concentrations than in plate-based cultures.

Furthermore, RNA sequencing of the exposed HepG2 cells revealed changes in biological pathways associated with TPhP-induced hepatotoxicity, including spliceosome and inflammatory signaling pathways. Overall, the experiments showed that the platform provides biological replicates without pooling, stable flow control and direct measurement of exposure profiles.

Linking toxicity to measured exposure

"Our platform can support human toxicity assessment based on real cell exposure, enabling next-generation risk assessment," remarks Kim. "Importantly, we measured the chemical concentrations in the system and followed their kinetics during exposure. This means that the toxicity observed can be tied to the concentration the cells actually experienced."

This work highlights how some practical challenges in applying OOCs may be addressed. The researchers hope that continued improvements will make the technology increasingly suitable for assessing or predicting chronic effects and other long-term toxicological outcomes.

content_html_zh:
Among the thousands of chemicals used in daily life, toxicity information is available for only a small fraction. Much of this information comes from high-dose animal studies, which are costly, time-consuming and limited by species differences.

Organ-on-a-chip (OOC) systems use microfluidics to mimic human tissue and organ physiology, offering a more human-relevant approach to toxicity testing. However, their application to toxicological assessment remains challenging due to issues with usability, flow control and biological replication. Complex tubing in flow-based OOC systems can further complicate their implementation.

To address these challenges, a research team involving professor Ki-Tae Kim and doctoral candidate Jiyun Kang from the Department of Environmental Engineering at Seoul National University of Science and Technology (SeoulTech) has developed a modular liver-on-a-chip (LOC) platform designed specifically for environmental toxicological assessment.

"The use of organ-on-a-chip platforms for environmental chemical assessment has advanced slowly, since testing many chemicals at multiple concentrations puts different demands on the system," explains Kim. "Our study offers insights into how these issues can be resolved and where these systems could be useful."

Their study was published in Environmental Science & Technology on Sept. 15, 2026.

Tubing-free chips with controlled flow

The proposed LOC platform accommodates 12 cartridge-based chips in parallel. It features a tubing-free design, with each chip incorporating an easy-to-use clamping-based sealing mechanism. A single LOC chip contains human liver HepG2 cultures and features independent unidirectional recirculating flow, with the flow rate and shear stress determined by gear-based peristaltic pumping.

Unlike static plate-based cultures, this recirculating flow continuously exposes cells to the circulating medium and enables controlled, reproducible chemical exposure, better reflecting biological conditions.

Liver responses at lower chemical concentrations

In tests, the LOC platform demonstrated stronger hepatic function than static plate cultures, with markedly higher expression of CYP1A2, CYP3A4 and CYP2E1 mRNA. The researchers used the LOC platform to evaluate the hepatotoxicity of triphenyl phosphate (TPhP), a common flame retardant used in household items with known links to liver toxicity.

During experiments, the cartridge modules demonstrated high reproducibility and uniform chemical distribution. In response to TPhP exposure, the platform showed changes in levels of hepatic phenotypic markers, including urea, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Notably, these altered responses were observed at lower measured concentrations than in plate-based cultures.

Furthermore, RNA sequencing of the exposed HepG2 cells revealed changes in biological pathways associated with TPhP-induced hepatotoxicity, including spliceosome and inflammatory signaling pathways. Overall, the experiments showed that the platform provides biological replicates without pooling, stable flow control and direct measurement of exposure profiles.

Linking toxicity to measured exposure

"Our platform can support human toxicity assessment based on real cell exposure, enabling next-generation risk assessment," remarks Kim. "Importantly, we measured the chemical concentrations in the system and followed their kinetics during exposure. This means that the toxicity observed can be tied to the concentration the cells actually experienced."

This work highlights how some practical challenges in applying OOCs may be addressed. The researchers hope that continued improvements will make the technology increasingly suitable for assessing or predicting chronic effects and other long-term toxicological outcomes.
